finding.claim: update_doc calls can_edit() but discards the boolean result instead of calling require_edit(), so there is no authorization check on document body updates. Any user can overwrite any document's body (broken access control / IDOR).
finding.source: Any request to PUT /doc/<doc_id> with a JSON body containing 'body'; doc_id is attacker-chosen and the caller needs no ownership or editor rights.
finding.sink: doc["body"] = request.json["body"] at docs.py:20, which writes to the shared DOCS store.

trace.note: Route PUT /doc/<doc_id> accepts an attacker-supplied doc_id
Document looked up by doc_id with no ownership scoping
can_edit(g.user, doc) result is ignored, so no abort(403) happens

finding.guards_checked: Compared with update_title (docs.py:27), which correctly uses require_edit and aborts with 403. update_doc has no such guard. No decorator or before_request hook exists in the file to enforce authorization. g.user is never set in this file, so authentication is assumed to come from elsewhere and is not visible here. Even if the user is authenticated, authorization is still missing.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: can_edit() at docs.py:19 returns a bool that is discarded; require_edit (which aborts 403) is used only in update_title at docs.py:27. No before_request or decorator exists in the directory.
verdict.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit(g.user, doc) as a bare statement, so docs.py:20 overwrites doc["body"] for any caller, whereas update_title uses require_edit at docs.py:27.

verdict_facts.guard_found: none (can_edit at docs.py:7-8 returns a bool that is discarded at line 19; the abort-based require_edit at line 11 is only used in update_title at line 27)
verdict_facts.reason: docs.py:19 calls can_edit() as a bare statement, so its bool result is never tested, and docs.py:20 writes the body for any authenticated user, whereas update_title at docs.py:27 correctly uses require_edit.
